errors.observed_error: Three defects made the Windows desktop layer look impossible. (1) The harness called GetClientRect with three arguments (byref(w), byref(h)) against a two-argument API, so the whole RECT landed in the first pointer and width/height were read back as left/top = 0. Every window therefore measured 0x0 and the GDI proof returned windows=0 on a machine where the real main window measures 1280x820 and visible=true. (2) Because (1) kept `found` empty, PrintWindow and GetBitmapBits were never executed on any machine, hiding two further defects: the GDI/DC functions declared argtypes but no restype, so a raw int was passed where wt.HDC was required, and GetBitmapBits received ctypes.byref(c_size_t(n)) where a DWORD value was required - both raise 'argument 2: TypeError: wrong type' the moment the path is finally reached. (3) check_9 probed only shutil.which('cargo') and ~/.cargo/bin/cargo.exe and then asserted 'Windows toolchain not installed' unconditionally, and GATE_SEMANTICS printed 'TAURI_WINDOWS_PENDING=yes(without Rust toolchain)'. That claim is false on this machine and contradicts the repository's own reference (windows-development-environment/references/tauri-build-shared-toolchain.md: 'Never turn a failed path probe into the persistent claim MSVC/Tauri is unavailable'), and register row AG-08 had promoted it to a machine-level blocker ('no Visual Studio and no VC tools at all').
errors.root_cause: Probe scope and dead code paths. The toolchain probe looked only at system PATH and the per-user cargo home, never at the declared shared roots in .project/governance/external-libraries-index.json (os-external), where MSVC 14.44.35207 (cl/link/MSBuild), a complete stable-x86_64-pc-windows-msvc toolchain with rustc.exe, cargo-tauri.exe and tauri-driver.exe all live; the Windows SDK import libraries are on the system volume at C:/Program Files (x86)/Windows Kits/10/Lib/10.0.28000.0/{ucrt,um}/x64. Separately, a Win32 signature error made the GDI branch always return an empty set, so the two downstream ctypes defects were unreachable and stayed latent from the day the harness was written.
errors.fix: Corrected all three at the root. check_9 now resolves cargo through the declared shared roots (external-libraries-index.json sharedRoots + libraries[kind=toolchains].assets[tool=cargo]) after an optional WORKLAB_CARGO override, PATH and ~/.cargo/bin, and performs a real 'cargo --version' readback, reporting the resolved path and version; the false unconditional 'Windows toolchain not installed' string is gone and the pending reason now names what is actually outstanding (desktop WebView2 E2E not executed). GATE_SEMANTICS no longer asserts 'without Rust toolchain'. The harness's GetClientRect now takes (HWND, LPRECT) and is wrapped in _client_size, and the GDI call chain got the restypes it was missing (GetDC/CreateCompatibleDC -> wt.HDC, CreateCompatibleBitmap -> wt.HBITMAP, SelectObject -> wt.HGDIOBJ, GetBitmapBits -> c_ulong, PrintWindow -> c_bool) with the count passed as a value. Positive readbacks from the same round: the shared toolchain compiled and RAN an msvc-target binary with zero downloads (RUSTC_EXIT=0, RUN_EXIT=0, 251,392 B), the Observer built with BUILD_EXIT=0 in 1m30s (app.exe 9,779,712 B, sha256 e659bbe9b20a2677, PE imports api-ms-win-crt-*/dwmapi with no libgcc/libwinpthread), and the app now stays ALIVE against the real sidecar instead of early-exiting 0xC0000135 as the previous GNU artifact did.
errors.regression_test: A Win32 wrapper must declare argtypes AND restype for every handle-returning call, and value parameters must be passed as values; a probe may not report a toolchain as absent unless every declared location in .project/governance/external-libraries-index.json has been probed and its exact path recorded in the evidence.
errors.repeat_prevention: Never record a machine-level blocker from a single-path probe: enumerate the declared shared roots and Windows Kits first and cite the paths attempted. Environment-limited branches must be executed at least once, because a branch that is never reached cannot fail and therefore cannot be trusted.
errors.remaining_boundary: Not yet closed: the real desktop surface proof. CDP over the process-level WEBVIEW2_ADDITIONAL_BROWSER_ARGUMENTS still yields no page target, so the probe window path (per-window additional_browser_args) is inert by architecture - WebView2 creates one browser environment per user-data folder and the main window creates it first. The corrected GDI proof has not yet produced a green verdict, so U19's desktop layer stays FAIL/PENDING and is not reported as passed. Full canonical gate after these edits: 47 gates PASS, exit 0.

errors.observed_error: Two open UI defects, 'the window-control cluster never renders' (P0-A) and 'the fourth KPI card is clipped at the right edge' (P0-B), were both readings of the instrument rather than of the app. Four separate defects in the capture harness produced them. (2) It captured GetWindowRect, which on a frameless window still includes the invisible resize border, so the image started 9px left and 1px above the client area. (3) It forced SetWindowPos to a PHYSICAL 1200x800 while Tauri declares window size in LOGICAL pixels, shrinking the real CSS viewport from 1280x820 to 946x632 and changing the layout under measurement - at 946px the KPI grid reflows to two columns, so the four-across row that 'proved' the clipping no longer existed. (4) A screen BitBlt cannot distinguish the app from whatever overlaps it: one capture showed a File Explorer window filling the content area and a centre pixel of pure white, and the pointer left inside the window also froze a hover-revealed tooltip that read as clipped text.
errors.root_cause: The instrument reported numbers but never proved its own assumptions: which artifact it launched, whether that artifact was current, which rectangle it photographed, what coordinate space that rectangle lived in, and whether anything was on top of it. Each assumption was inherited from the previous run's guess, and every downstream breakpoint conclusion was stated as though measured. The one genuine layout defect the region did contain - .topbar reserving 210px for a cluster that is ~269 CSS px wide once the zoom group appears above 1240px, letting the transport truth strip slide under the caption buttons - was invisible because the captures never showed the real viewport.
errors.fix: New instrument .project-local/runs/p0a-diag-20261006/shot3.py: resolves the launched exe from every candidate target dir and refuses to run unless it is newer than tauri.conf.json, Cargo.toml, src/*.rs and frontend/dist/** (STALE_OR_MISSING_BINARY otherwise); makes the process per-monitor-DPI-aware and records before/after; captures GetClientRect + ClientToScreen instead of GetWindowRect and fails if the client size disagrees with DWMWA_EXTENDED_FRAME_BOUNDS by more than 3px; moves with SWP_NOSIZE so the app's own logical size is what gets judged; photographs the same rect twice, once by screen BitBlt and once by PrintWindow(PW_CLIENTONLY|PW_RENDERFULLCONTENT), reports the differing-pixel ratio, and treats PrintWindow as authoritative when they disagree (occlusion) or the BitBlt is covered; parks the pointer outside the window before launch and restores it; and reports right-edge ink bands so clipping is measured rather than eyeballed. Product fix: .topbar now reserves 130px, switching to 285px at min-width 1241px - the same width at which the zoom group appears - and the stale unconditional 210px declaration was deleted rather than overridden. Zoom buttons switched from Minus/Plus to ZoomOut/ZoomIn, which had made two identical minus glyphs sit in one pill meaning 'zoom out' and 'minimize'.
errors.regression_test: shot3.py exits non-zero on STALE_OR_MISSING_BINARY, INSTRUMENT_INVALID or a blank capture, and writes capture-provenance.json with the artifact sha256 it launched; a layout conclusion may only be recorded from a run whose instrumentDisagreements is empty and whose captureCrossCheck.differingPixelRatio is near zero. errors.observed_error: The GDI capture rectangle was derived from the comparison 'w * 12 >= WINDOW_LOGICAL_WIDTH_PX * dpi', a typo for * 96. On this machine GetClientRect already returns PHYSICAL pixels because the instrument had just made itself per-monitor DPI aware (main window reads 1600x1025 at GetDpiForWindow = 120, i.e. 1280x820 logical x 1.25), so the comparison wrongly concluded the value was still logical, scaled it by 1.25 a second time and allocated 2000x1281 for a 1600x1025 client area. BitBlt then copied 400x256 px of desktop and neighbouring windows past the subject's right and bottom edges. That foreign content made a window painting nothing but its own #08090a background read as 375, 635, 722 and 384 distinct colours across four windows, and a first-cut conclusion that the screen BitBlt had captured the real UI was recorded on that basis before the rectangle was checked.
errors.root_cause: The instrument inferred its coordinate space from a number instead of from the DPI-awareness state it had itself set, and it never bounded the capture rectangle by the client area it had measured microseconds earlier. Both failures point the same way: a capture larger than its subject photographs the surroundings and manufactures content that belongs to no application.
errors.fix: Scale is applied only when SetProcessDpiAwarenessContext(PER_MONITOR_AWARE_V2) did not take effect, and that fact is recorded per run as dpiAwareProcess. The requested rectangle is now clamped with min(w, round(w * scale)) and min(h, round(h * scale)), so it can never exceed the measured client area. Every window entry records sizeAsRead, captureSize, scaleApplied, dpi and expectedPhysicalWIfMain so the coordinate space is auditable after the fact.
errors.regression_test: python scripts/ci/failfast_group.py --group observer-python-skeleton plus the GDI stage of python apps/observer/scripts/u19_webview_e2e.py: every window entry must satisfy captureSize <= sizeAsRead. Re-running the corrected instrument against the same binary returned 41 distinct colours at #08090a 99.99% dominant, in place of the forged 375-722, which is the regression assertion.
errors.repeat_prevention: Every capture must record the coordinate space it believes it is in and the rectangle it used, and that rectangle must never exceed the client area measured in the same run; a capture larger than its subject must be rejected rather than read, because it photographs the desktop and forges evidence.
errors.remaining_boundary: Only the 1280x820 main and 440x780 panel windows were measured, so other resize states remain unmeasured. PrintWindow still cannot photograph the WebView2 surface (1-2 distinct colours across all four flags at both sizes), so the screen BitBlt remains the only working capture path and still depends on z-order.

No error, no visual change. The window itself renders the full interface, which also disproves the blank-release conclusion in ERR-102.
errors.root_cause: Tauri v2 denies every mutating window and webview command by default. The compiled capability was [core:default, core:window:allow-start-dragging], and core:window:default in the build's own ACL manifest lists only readers (allow-is-maximized, allow-inner-size, allow-title and friends); allow-minimize, allow-toggle-maximize, allow-close and core:webview:allow-set-webview-zoom are separate identifiers that were never granted, so each click rejected at the ACL boundary. The rejection was then erased twice over: WindowControls called the API without awaiting it, so the rejected promise bypassed its own try/catch and surfaced as an unhandled rejection, and the catch body was empty.
errors.fix: Granted exactly the four identifiers the shipped UI actually calls: core:window:allow-minimize, core:window:allow-toggle-maximize, core:window:allow-close, core:webview:allow-set-webview-zoom; and awaited each native call so a future denial cannot vanish silently. No other permission was added: the read-only-surface assertion in the same suite still forbids shell/fs/http/process grants.

Both failure modes were injected and observed to fail before the gate was trusted.
errors.repeat_prevention: Any UI call into the native shell must be awaited and must appear in the capability-contract map, because a Tauri v2 permission that is not granted fails as an asynchronous rejection that no synchronous try/catch will ever see. Capability grants must be derived from calls, never from a feature list.

errors.observed_error: The probe's own gate asked only that registrySha256 be 64 characters long, and the probe computed it over the working tree. Under `* text=auto` that value differs between this machine (CRLF) and the runner (LF), so the receipt's pin was unrepeatable across machines and could not be checked anywhere. It then went stale in a way I produced myself: after re-pointing hermes I ran the probe without --out, the printed summary was current while the shipped receipt still pinned the older registry and quoted the superseded version, and every test stayed green.
errors.root_cause: A digest claim was recorded without a basis and without a comparator. Length-64 reads as 'a hash is present' and hides both which bytes it names and whether the file still matches - the ERR-125 family, and the reason ERR-153 moved digest resolution to the index: the object that ships is the index blob, not the bytes on my disk.
errors.fix: registry_pin() now hashes the git index first, then HEAD, then the working tree, and names the basis in the receipt (git-index). The gate compares that pin against the same resolution and refuses a receipt that describes a different registry than the tree carries. Falsified by drifting the registry under a stale receipt (red) and restoring byte-for-byte (green again), and the assertion first fired on the real defect: the working-tree pin did not equal the index blob, which is the machine-dependence being removed.
errors.repeat_prevention: A published digest must state which object it names, and a gate must re-derive and compare it rather than check its shape. When a tool can run without writing its artifact, the artifact and the state it describes must be compared, or a fresh printout will silently coexist with a stale receipt.
errors.remaining_boundary: The comparison catches a receipt generated against different registry bytes; it does not detect a receipt that is current but whose *rows* were hand-edited, nor does it force anyone to re-run the probe with --out (running it without output still succeeds by design). The probe's per-row claims about binaries outside the repository remain machine-local and are readback-guarded, not CI-enforced.

errors.observed_error: Both servers promise that every write verb is refused with 405, and the promise was unreachable for a caller that had already sent a body: the refusal was written while the request bytes were still in the socket buffer, so a keep-alive client's next read began with its own JSON instead of a status line. The visible symptom was a governance-batch error in test_write_methods_other_than_the_single_post_are_405 with three server-side ConnectionResetError [WinError 10054] tracebacks, while the same module passed five consecutive standalone runs -- the signature of a transport-level defect that only appears under connection reuse.
errors.root_cause: The 405 was treated as the whole contract, when the contract is a *parseable response*. Nothing in the suite spoke raw bytes, so every assertion went through a parser that hides what actually arrives first. The Observer sidecar runs HTTP/1.1 where the control server does not, so the exposure differed per server and neither was tested at the byte level.
errors.fix: The request body is read at most once and cached (`_read_request_body`): the POST path consumes the operation, a refusal clears the buffer, and a body over MAX_BODY_BYTES is never buffered at all. Both servers close the connection rather than risk misalignment. The sidecar keeps the 405 spelled out inside each do_<verb> body because verify_observer_readonly_boundary.py reads those bodies -- routing the denial through the shared helper alone made the guard go red, which is the guard working, not failing. A new raw-socket test asserts the status line precedes any echoed body. My first attempt put the drain in _send, which made the success path read Content-Length twice and block; caught by running the suite three times, and the reason the accessor exists.
errors.repeat_prevention: Any server that answers a write verb must be asserted at the byte level, not only through a client parser: a test that opens a raw socket and reads the response proves the status line came first. And when a source-shape guard fires on a refactor, change the call site, never the check.
errors.remaining_boundary: The sidecar's own keep-alive byte-level test is not written: its handler class is nested inside the serving function, so the assertion needs a subprocess boot like the browser-entry tests use. The drain is in place there, but only the control server has a proof at the byte level. 2026-10-08 更正并闭合：本节所说「sidecar 的 byte 级 keep-alive 测试需要子进程启动，因为 handler 类嵌在 serving 函数里」不成立——`create_server` 是模块级函数且可绑 0 端口，测试在同进程内直接对它说话即可。新增 tests/workflow-assistance/test_sidecar_write_refusal_bytes_keepalive.py：一条 keep-alive 连接上先 POST 被拒（405，body 未被回显），再 GET 必须干净地拿到 `HTTP/1.1 200 OK`；并附一个故意不 drain 的对照服务器，实测第二次响应不再是干净状态行，从而证明这条断言可以失败。连跑 3 次稳定。

errors.root_cause: Parent and child disagreed about the encoding of the same byte stream, and the failure surfaced five frames away from its cause. `subprocess.run(..., text=True)` with no `encoding=` decodes with the locale, which on this host is cp936, while Chinese-printing scripts have to run with `PYTHONIOENCODING=utf-8` -- the batch inherited that, so the child wrote UTF-8 and the parent decoded GBK. At byte 0xaf of offset 88824 subprocess's own `_readerthread` raised UnicodeDecodeError; the threading module printed it and the thread died, so `communicate()` returned None for that stream. Measured in one call: stdout was a str of 100,374 characters while stderr was None. On CI the locale is already UTF-8, so the runner there could never reproduce this.
errors.fix: Both ends pinned, then the whole class closed the same day. In the gate runner: its 8 text-mode pipes pass encoding='utf-8', errors='replace' (the two governance-batch calls and six git calls, including the best-effort `_git` helper whose None stream would have been swallowed into an empty identity), and `_run_governance_batch` sets env['PYTHONIOENCODING'] = 'utf-8' for the children whose output it reads. The three tests that crashed on a None stream were victims of the same mechanism, not failed assertions. Then the next gate in the same run (`run_root_governance_suite.py`) failed on the identical line shape, which proved the narrow declared-set approach was the wrong scope -- the class recurs wherever a text pipe exists, so the sweep went tree-wide: the remaining 100 sites across 61 tracked files now declare an encoding, inserted mechanically at the `text=` keyword's own end column and validated by re-parsing before writing (diff shape: 88+ / 88- then 12+ / 12-, one line changed per site, no line-ending churn). Measured after the sweep: 642 tracked Python files, 223 text-mode pipes, 0 undeclared, 0 unreadable. The guard enforces that over every tracked file with no exemption list, carries positive and negative controls (a bad shape is flagged, a declared one is not, a bytes-mode `text=False` call and a non-subprocess `.run(...)` are invisible), fails when a tracked file cannot be parsed so an unreadable file cannot hide a violation, and keeps a 150-pipe capability floor so an empty offender list means the rule holds rather than the scanner going blind.
errors.regressionTestVerifiabilityReason: AST over a tracked module plus injected good/bad sources; no host locale is consulted, so it judges the same way on CI
errors.repeat_prevention: a tool that reads a child process in text mode must declare the encoding at both ends, and a gate whose verdict becomes a receipt must never depend on the host locale agreeing by accident; when a gate crashes instead of printing a failure, suspect the harness's own pipes before suspecting the subject, because a decode error raised inside a subprocess reader thread arrives as a None stream, not as a codec message anyone can read
errors.remaining_boundary: `errors='replace'` trades a crash for a visibly degraded log: where a child legitimately writes the host codepage, its output now shows replacement characters instead of decoding correctly. errors.repeat_prevention: a status token must state a falsifiable quantity, never an absence: 'CI not run' cannot be contradicted by anything and therefore survives being wrong, while 'red: 4 of 24' invites the re-check. errors.observed_error: A guard I had written, run and reported as green (8/8, three times) failed inside the canonical batch: test_the_context_pack_renders_identically_twice_and_names_no_secret asserted two renders of the handoff context pack were byte-identical. errors.root_cause: I asserted a property the artifact cannot have (byte identity across time) and the assertion's truth depended on wall-clock luck, which is not a tested property. The same file already contained the correct shape one case earlier -- the current-state check names the one line allowed to move and convicts every other difference -- and I did not apply it to the pack. Running the module standalone also hid the timing: a fast solo run keeps two subprocess calls inside one second, while the batch runs them under load. I reported the standalone pass as evidence without stating its timing assumption.
errors.fix: Rewritten as a stability claim that is actually testable: exactly one '- Generated UTC:' line must exist in each render (so the exclusion cannot silently excuse a second stamp), the renders must be compared with that line removed, every other line must be byte-equal, and the pack must still name the branch and HEAD it was rendered from. The assertion no longer depends on when it runs; verified by three consecutive module runs and then by the batch itself.
errors.regression_test: tests/workflow-assistance/test_agent_default_material_is_regenerated_and_current.py (test_the_context_pack_moves_only_its_generation_stamp_between_renders). The stability of the corrected case is itself checked by running the module three times in a row; the batch run is what exposed the original fault.
errors.repeat_prevention: A comparison across two runs of a generated artifact must name the field that is allowed to move and compare everything else, never assert byte identity -- and a timing-dependent assertion must be proven by at least one slow path (the batch), not only by a fast solo run. Before quoting a fresh test as green, ask what would make it red at a different time of day.
errors.remaining_boundary: Nothing enforces that future generated artifacts declare their timestamp field to the comparing test; a second pack that prints two stamps would only be caught by the 'exactly one stamp' assertion I added here, which is per-artifact.

(1) The census disposition I published told the next agent to fix the references to the six historical root documents and then move them, because it had counted only documentation as a consumer. Moving the file exactly as my own instruction said would have disarmed a negative control and made a ledger record describe a path that no longer exists. (2) I wrote a count of 18 referrers into that section before measuring anything with a stated scope; the number was a recollection of a listing, and the measured values are 21 for the scope above and 24 once yaml/yml are included. (3) The guard I had shipped minutes earlier, tests/workflow-assistance/test_default_load_doc_citations_resolve.py, asserts that every citation in the default-load chain resolves or is declared a class reference, and it returned exit 0 while my own census edit contained the bare token `test_control_service.py` - a path no reader can open from the repository root. The normaliser had been printing rewritten=1 the whole time and nothing read that field.
errors.root_cause: Two confusions. First, a consumer of a filename is not only prose that cites it: a test can depend on a file existing with a particular spelling, and a ledger record can depend on that name being quoted truthfully, and neither appears in a reference search aimed at documentation. Second, resolvable and readable-from-the-root are different predicates, and I wrote the assertion for the weaker one while the comment claimed the stronger; a tool that already publishes a second counter (rewritten) invites exactly this, because the gate reads the counter it was written against and the other one silently describes the defect.
errors.fix: The disposition changed from move to label-in-place, with the blocking evidence measured and written out: .project/governance/root-document-dispositions.json classifies all 11 tracked root Markdown files (authority=2, convention-current=3, historical-non-normative=6), scripts/ci/verify_root_document_dispositions.py derives the authority set from project-authority-index.json instead of copying it, requires the visible NON-NORMATIVE-HISTORICAL marker inside the first twelve lines, requires the banner to name the index's currentTaskpack verbatim, and proves that removing the banner reproduces the committed bytes exactly - so the acceptance rule about preserving original bytes became a checked claim instead of an intention. Six banners of +481 B were inserted; the mandatory gate tests/workflow-assistance/test_root_document_dispositions.py has 14 cases including two falsifications on real files (drop a banner, append to a body), each restored byte-identically at 13,210 B and 10,255 B. The unscoped 18 was rewritten with its scope stated. And test_the_chain_is_normalised_not_merely_resolvable now requires rewritten == 0, falsified by re-introducing a shorthand citation into a scoped document: gate exit 1 naming that test, file restored identical at 21,011 B, suite back to 6/6 OK (.project-local/runs/falsify_normalised_citation_assertion.py).
errors.repeat_prevention: Before proposing to move or rename any file, enumerate consumers over the whole tracked tree and read each hit for the reason it depends on the name - a test fixture and a quoted ledger record are consumers even though neither cites the file as a location. Every counter a tool publishes must either be asserted by the gate that digests it or removed, because an unread field is decoration. A count must never be written without the scope command that produced it.
errors.remaining_boundary: The gate judges that a citation can be followed from the repository root, not that the sentence around it is true. Whether the six historical files eventually move to docs/history/archive/ stays an owner decision - it now has the consumer list and the byte-preservation proof attached, and the banner makes a mistaken pickup survivable rather than impossible.

errors.observed_error: The citation guard I shipped for the default-load chain was narrower than the chain it claims to cover, in two independent ways. (1) Its scope was eight documents described as 'the order AGENTS.md prescribes for resolving authority', but step 6 of that bootstrap is taskpacks/current/OPEN-TASK-REGISTER.md — the one document this round writes its findings into — and it was not in SCOPE. The moment it was, the run reported 374 citations in nine documents, 80 in a shape a reader cannot follow from the repository root, and 9 citations that resolve to nothing at all: seven bare evidence-receipt filenames whose directory was named only earlier in the sentence, and two paths quoted in order to say they were wrong. (2) The population those citations are matched against was built by walking a hand-written SOURCE_DIRS allowlist of eleven roots. It measured 2,474 paths and did not contain projections/agents/generate.py, which is tracked and is cited by the WUI-16 row, so an honest citation was reported as unresolved; the same blindness hid every tracked file under any root I had not thought to list. Widening the walk then produced a second, opposite defect: .ui-reference/WORK-LAB/** carries inbound copies with the same basenames (types.ts, navigation.ts), so two correct citations turned red as 'ambiguous' once those bytes entered the basename index.
errors.root_cause: An allowlist stood in for measurement twice over — a list of directories in place of the checkout, and a list of documents in place of the authority bootstrap the scope claimed to implement. Both fail the same way: what is absent from the list is invisible to the verdict, so the guard reports a clean chain while the chain it actually reads is smaller than the one agents load. The inbound-copy ambiguity is the mirror image: a basename index must be scoped to files that can be a navigation target, not to every byte on disk.
errors.fix: Population is now the checkout: `git ls-files` unioned with a repository-wide walk (runtime root `.project-local` excluded so a local copy can never decide what a bare name means; measured 2,474 to 2,700 paths), and frozen trees plus inbound reference copies stay citable as explicit paths but are kept out of the basename index via NOT_INDEXED_PREFIXES. SCOPE gained the live register. The register's seven bare receipt names were rewritten to their full .project-local/artifacts/wui-20261009/ paths (7 substitutions across 6 names, each asserted on the written bytes), and the two paths quoted as defects are now excused by a QUOTED_AS_ABSENT allowlist matched on the full citation token with a stated reason, validated as used, so an allowance that excuses no current text turns the run red instead of quietly excusing the next real error. After --apply the chain reads docs=9 citations=365 rewritten=0 blocked=0 generic_allowed=14 absent_quoted=2 stale_allowances=0. Three new cases in tests/workflow-assistance/test_default_load_doc_citations_resolve.py hold the line (register in scope, tracked files visible regardless of directory, no inbound copy as a bare-name meaning), and all three were falsified by mutating the tool itself: dropping the reference exclusion gave failures=1 on its own case, restricting the walk to one root gave failures=2, and the tool was restored byte-identically and re-run green 8/8 after each (.project-local/runs/falsify_citation_cases.py).
errors.repeat_prevention: A scope that names itself after an authority procedure must be derived from that procedure, not from a remembered list: re-read the bootstrap steps and assert each one is present in the scope. A file population must come from the tracked manifest or the filesystem, never from an allowlist of directories, because the failure is silence about what the list omits. When a wider population produces new reds, check whether the added bytes can legitimately be a navigation target before treating the red as a defect in the document.
errors.remaining_boundary: The rewrite makes every citation followable; it does not make the sentence true. The register still cites runtime receipts that a clean checkout does not carry, which the guard exempts by name rather than silently — and on the machine that wrote them their absence is a failure, so the exemption is checked rather than assumed.

errors.observed_error: Three tracked CLIs and one worker entry point wrote or accepted the canonical store outside the project root. `collectors.py:332`, `active_projects.py:204` and `project_registry.py:168` each defaulted `--runtime-root` to `Path(tempfile.gettempdir()) / "workflow-assistance-*"` and then created `canonical.sqlite` there, while `durable_worker.py` required `--runtime-root` but accepted any value it was handed. `.project/governance/project-data-boundary.json` declares `runtimeRoot: .project-local/runs` and AGENTS.md requires everything this project produces to stay inside the Git root, so a bare invocation of any of the four spilled durable state into the user's temp directory, where the boundary sweep does not look and the checkout does not reach. Measured on this machine: zero `workflow-assistance-*` directories in C:\Windows\TEMP, %LOCALAPPDATA%\Temp and TMP -- the defect was latent, never exercised here, which is exactly why it survived.
errors.root_cause: A declared boundary was written as a document instead of a predicate. Every module that needed a runtime root re-implemented the choice locally, and the default was the convenient one; nothing on the entry path asked whether the resulting path was inside the repository. A spill rule that lives only in prose is invisible to the code that spills.
errors.fix: One shared predicate in `packages/client-neutral-core/scripts/project_temp.py`: `declared_runtime_root()` reads `runtimeRoot` from the boundary contract, `runtime_dir(name)` hangs a named directory under it, and `require_runtime_root(value, name)` accepts a caller-supplied root only after proving containment -- and raises `RUNTIME_ROOT_ESCAPES_PROJECT` before any mkdir. All four entry points now call it, so none keeps its own copy of the decision. Mandatory gate `tests/workflow-assistance/test_worker_runtime_roots_stay_inside_the_project.py` (6 cases) scans tracked source for the defect's AST shape (an assignment to a `*runtime_root*` name whose value reaches `gettempdir()`) rather than for any mention of temp, so the residue cleaner that legitimately empties `%TEMP%` is not convicted; it also runs the worker CLI against an outside root and requires the named refusal with nothing created. Falsified by re-shipping the defect into `project_registry.py`: gate exit 1 naming `packages/client-neutral-core/scripts/project_registry.py:168`, module restored byte-identically, 6/6 green again (.project-local/runs/falsify_runtime_root_scan.py).
errors.repeat_prevention: A path policy must be one callable that every entry point uses, never a convention each file re-derives; an enforcement test must refuse a path that is outside by construction (the repository's own parent), not one taken from `tempfile.gettempdir()`, because the canonical gate runner binds TMP/TEMP/TMPDIR inside the project and a temp-derived 'outside' probe silently tests nothing. A falsifier that exits non-zero is not evidence until it names the fault: two probes this round died of their own harness (a doubled cwd, and an LF anchor against a CRLF file) and both were caught only by asserting the finding text.
errors.remaining_boundary: The scan convicts the shape it was written against -- an assignment feeding `gettempdir()` into a runtime root. A root computed some other way (a literal path, an environment variable read directly) is outside its vocabulary, so the worker's runtime root stays covered by the CLI refusal rather than by the scan alone.

errors.observed_error: The canonical store screened field NAMES and never field VALUES, so a provider token carried under an allowed key was written to durable state: `collect_usage_files` turns each line of a `usage.jsonl` file into a canonical record whose `provider`/`model`/`note` strings come straight from the foreign file. When I added the missing value check, my first version was too strict and an existing test convicted it on the first run: `test_task_loop_retries_then_blocks_on_repeated_failure` died with `sensitive value(s) at: ['checkpoint.error_fingerprint']`, because the blob pattern that catches a base64 secret also matches any 64-or-longer alphanumeric run -- which in this repository means SHA-256 fingerprints, commit SHAs and generated ids. Had the suite not covered that path, the guard would have broken the worker's own task loop.
errors.root_cause: One pattern serving two different questions. For an artifact-transfer decision the strict reading is right (quarantine is cheap and a lookalike blob deserves suspicion); for ingest into canonical state the same reading refuses ordinary data, because this project's identities are hexadecimal digests. Copying the artifact-flow answer into the store imported the wrong cost model with it.
errors.fix: Two functions over one pattern set in `artifact_flow_policy.py`: `find_nested_secrets` (unchanged, still what the flow decision uses) and `secret_value_paths`, which applies the same credential shapes minus an explicit digest exemption -- a value of only hexadecimal, 32+ characters, is treated as what it is here. `validate_record` calls the new function after the name scan, so `canonical_store.py:113-119` now refuses a value-shaped credential at every write. New mandatory gate `tests/workflow-assistance/test_canary_synthetic_secret_never_reaches_the_store.py` (4 cases): five planted synthetic shapes refused in three allowed fields (15 combinations) and in a bare string inside a list (`tags[1]`); digests and prose carrying the word 'token' accepted; and the end-to-end canary -- a fixture `usage.jsonl` with one poisoned and one honest line, collected by the real collector, where ingest refuses exactly one row, keeps the honest one, and the planted key appears in neither `list_usage_samples()` nor `projection()`. Falsified by deleting the value scan: gate exit 1 with failures=3 naming 'the planted provider-key shape in provider was accepted by validate_record'; store restored byte-identically (CRLF preserved, 54,695 B) and the canary, `test_durable_worker` (8), `test_collectors` (7) and `test_snapshot_sse_live` (25) all green afterwards (.project-local/runs/falsify_canary_value_scan.py).
errors.repeat_prevention: When a stricter check is added to a write path, run the path's own suite before writing the guard's tests, and size the pattern to the question the code is answering: share the vocabulary of secret shapes but not the decision policy between an artifact-transfer gate and an ingest gate. A guard that rejects the system's own identifiers is a defect in the guard, never in the data. And never plant a fixture shorter than the pattern it is meant to trip -- a 63-character blob quietly matched nothing, so the first red I saw was my own test being inert.
errors.remaining_boundary: Refusal at ingest is strict by design: one poisoned line inside a collected file raises, the tick records a collector failure, and the circuit breaker eventually opens for that collector -- so a hostile source degrades collection visibly instead of being silently filtered. The value shapes are the artifact-flow set (provider prefixes, bearer, long base64), not a general entropy detector, and a short or unusual credential format can still pass as an ordinary string.

(1) Moving `token_monitor.py`'s self-test onto the new `project_temp.fixture_root()` helper gave it the prefix `token-monitor-selftest-`, which the evidence reader refuses because the name contains `token`; the helper then raised after five consecutive refused roots. The census gate that exists precisely to stop this -- tests/workflow-assistance/test_fixture_root_names_are_readable_by_the_reader.py -- stayed green, because its AST matcher recognises only calls named `fixture_dir`. A gate whose vocabulary predates the helper I added cannot see the helper. (2) To check the converted modules I ran each one as `python <module>.py`. `token_monitor.py` with no `--self-test` launches its tkinter GUI, so a window opened on the owner's desktop and sat there until the 180-second subprocess timeout killed it -- the repository rule is explicitly not to raise interfaces repeatedly, and the headless flag was one `argparse` line away that I did not read. (3) The background task's completion notice reported `exit code 0` for that run while the runner itself had died on TimeoutExpired: the notification described the wrapper, not the work, and none of the other six modules' self-test results were ever printed.
errors.root_cause: The census was written against a name rather than a property: it enumerates the helper that existed when it was authored, so any new helper that forwards to the same sensitive-name rule is invisible to it. The GUI launch is the same failure in a different costume -- running a module without reading its entry point, i.e. treating a filename as a description of what it does. And trusting a wrapper status as a verdict is the oldest error in this ledger.
errors.fix: The prefix became `monitor-selftest-` (verified against `name_is_sensitive` directly before and after), and the census now accepts both `fixture_dir` and `fixture_root` with a comment recording why the vocabulary had to grow. The extension was falsified by planting the credential-shaped prefix `auth-store-` at the real call site: the gate produced failures=1 naming `packages\client-neutral-core\scripts\token_monitor.py:240 prefix='auth-store-'`, the module was restored byte-identically, and the class ran green afterwards (.project-local/runs/falsify_fixture_prefix_census.py). Every tracked module with a GUI default is now run only through its `--self-test` flag or its test suite.
errors.repeat_prevention: When new code adopts a helper that an existing gate audits by name, the gate must be extended in the same change -- an auditor that lists yesterday's function names is decoration -- and the extension must be falsified against a planted bad call site. Before executing any tracked module, read its `main()` for a GUI or long-running default and use the headless flag. A background completion notice is not a result: only the emitted verdict counts.
errors.remaining_boundary: The census reads literal prefixes only; a prefix assembled at runtime (an f-string or a variable) is still outside its reach, and the helper's own refusal loop remains the last line for that shape.

errors.observed_error: The governance batch turned a fourth red today, and it was a real one in an instrument I trust: `test_the_debt_figure_is_reported_as_debt_not_progress` failed with `AssertionError: 6 not less than or equal to 5`. The unbound-record triage classifies a PASS row as a clear binding candidate when its guard file resolves and its first commit sits within the date window of the record. ERR-245 joined that list -- but the record it describes was written today, its fix is in the uncommitted working set, and the `guardFirstCommit` that made it look eligible belongs to a test file that existed two days before the fix it is now being used to prove. Proximity was coincidence. Had the ceiling been 6 instead, the audit would have published a candidate with no commit that carries the record at all.
errors.root_cause: The candidate rule consulted the guard file's history and the record's date, but never asked the one question a binding depends on: does a commit exist that carries this record? The tool already computes exactly that (the birth-commit pass, `git log -S "<error_id>"` on the ledger) and used it only for the separate `bindableByBirthCommit` partition, so the two partitions were built on different evidence and the weaker one could call an uncommitted record a candidate.
errors.fix: `scripts/audit/triage_unbound_ledger_records.py` now settles the window after the birth pass: an in-window record with no birth commit moves to a new named partition `heldForUncommittedRecord` (`heldForUncommittedRecord` in `counts` too), so it is reported as held rather than as a candidate whose SHA has merely not been written yet. Measured after the change: `clear 0 heldUncommitted 6 undated 32 distant 4 bindableByBirth 0`, with `RESOLVES 42 = 0 + 6 + 32 + 4` still exhaustive -- the partition is a reshuffle of the same population, not a reduction of the debt, and `unboundPassRecords` stays 116. The gate adds both directions of the rule to its assertions (a candidate must have a birth commit; a held record must not, and must still carry a date delta), and 8/8 green. The typed ceiling of five is kept on purpose and the comment now states when it will bite: when this working set is committed, up to six records can become genuine candidates at once, and that is the moment to re-derive the ceiling from the commit graph rather than to raise a number until the run goes green.
errors.repeat_prevention: A classification that produces a commit must require the commit's existence, not a proxy for it; when a tool already computes the stronger signal for one partition, every other partition must consume the same signal rather than a near-neighbour of it. A ceiling that an honest new record can breach is a finding about the record, not a number to adjust -- and never widen a bound to make a run green, because the bound is the only thing that made the run meaningful.
errors.remaining_boundary: `heldForUncommittedRecord` is accurate only while the working set is uncommitted: once these rows are committed, the same rule will promote them, and whether each promotion is legitimate then depends on the commit actually carrying the fix, which the gate cannot see before the commit exists. That check is the binding tool's job at commit time.

errors.observed_error: The interface-binding matrix and acceptance checklist failed their own citation gate two ways at once. `test_every_citation_resolves_or_is_declared_absent` reported 59 problems, and `test_every_line_pointer_lands_on_the_code_it_quotes` reported `AssertionError: 106 not greater than or equal to 140` -- the census had collapsed from the 144 line-bearing citations the file actually carries. Probing the two counts against the tree showed they were the same defect: 58 of 233 citations were written as a bare basename (`composition_root.py:285`) or with a directory that does not exist (`services/control/handoff.py:31`, `services/orchestration/impact_planner.py:136`, `services/orchestration/perf_baseline.py:42`, `scripts/single_field_apply_loop.py:130`, `src/usageCache.contract.test.tsx:10`, `packages/.../project_identity_resolver.py:75`), and a pointer whose path cannot be opened from the repository root is silently skipped by the content check. So 38 of 144 pointers had never been read -- including six that named a wrong directory, which is a false provenance claim, not a formatting nicety. Once the paths were resolved, eight pointers then failed the content check on their line number (off by 1 to 4 lines, one of them `perf_baseline.py:42` because this session deleted and added lines in that file), and one citation, `apps/observer/frontend/src/lib/shared_rule_adaptation.ts:5-6` in B34's evidence field, names a file that has never existed in this repository -- the ERR-239 shape again, a path transcribed from a subagent report and used as if it proved a claim.
errors.root_cause: The two CSVs were filled from research reports whose authors wrote paths relative to their own module, and the fill step copied those strings without resolving them against the repository root. The citation guard that was written afterwards checked path *existence* only when it could open the path, and treated an unopenable path as out of scope rather than as a finding -- so the shorthand both broke the first assertion and hid evidence from the second. The B34 row is the same failure one level up: a citation was accepted as provenance because nobody opened it.
errors.fix: Every unresolved citation was expanded against the tree by `.project-local/runs/wui-20261010/expand_shorthand_citations.py`, which derives its replacement map from the gate's own scan (so prose mentioning `package.json` is not relabelled), refuses to write unless the basename has exactly one file behind it, and content-verifies each wrong-directory pointer before adopting the candidate (`line 136 window holds the quoted code`). 43 distinct tokens were rewritten; `ui_read_model.ts` was deliberately expanded to the pack copy under `docs/history/owner-inputs/20261009/ui-readable/contracts/`, because the B02 sentence says the v1 pack and the repository has no production file of that name. B34's dead path became `ABSENT:` and now cites `apps/observer/frontend/src/lib/ruleProjectionTruth.ts:34`, which really does re-declare PROJECTED / NULL_FIELD / SOURCE_GAP, alongside the honest limit that config-ownership field ownership is not projected. Eight drifted pointers were moved by `repoint_convicted_pointers.py`, which only moves a pointer the gate itself convicted, only onto a line that uniquely holds the quoted code within 30 lines, and re-runs the gate's predicate on the written bytes. Measured after: 234 citations -- 223 resolve, 10 runtime receipts, 1 declared absent, 0 unresolved; 144 pointers checked, 0 problems. Both floors held; neither was lowered.
errors.repeat_prevention: A citation must be resolved from the repository root at the moment it is written, not at review time; a checker that skips what it cannot open must report the skip as a count, because an invisible population is how a census quietly drops from 144 to 106 while still printing a green-looking number. Any path copied from a report must be opened before it is used as evidence, and a claim that a file does not exist must be written as an explicit ABSENT marker rather than left as a plausible path.
errors.remaining_boundary: The expansion proves the cited file exists and the cited line holds the quoted code; it does not prove the surrounding sentence's interpretation of that code. Six citations had a directory that does not exist, and each was accepted only because its line content matched -- a citation with a wrong directory and no line number would still pass. B34's rewrite also records that the truth vocabulary and the config-ownership vocabulary are two different three-state sets, which the original row conflated.

errors.observed_error: Two of my own write-path defects in one hour. First: seven matrix line pointers were repaired earlier today and the repair tool printed a receipt saying so, yet the file on disk still carried all seven pre-repair numbers when the gate re-read it -- a later script rewrote the whole CSV from a copy it had loaded itself, so the shipped bytes no longer matched the receipt. Second: the citation expansion I ran today substituted a replacement sentence into the raw file text, and that sentence contained a comma. The `evidence` field is not quoted in this CSV, so row B34 grew from 14 columns to 15 and the table became unreadable as a table -- and no assertion in the gate noticed, because `csv.DictReader` parks a surplus field under a `None` key and the header-name and row-count checks both still passed.
errors.root_cause: The first defect is a verification ordering mistake: each write was checked right after its own write, but the last writer in a chain of scripts wins, and nothing re-read the shipped bytes after the final write. The second is editing a delimited format as if it were free text -- the substitution was safe for paths, which cannot contain a comma, and unsafe for sentences, and the guard that should have caught it asserted the header and the row count instead of the per-row field count.
errors.fix: The re-point tool now ends by calling the gate's own `pointer_findings` against the file as written and prints `BEFORE checked= 144 problems= 8` / `AFTER checked= 144 problems= 0`, so a receipt that the bytes do not support cannot be produced. B34's sentence was rewritten with semicolons only and the write is now validated by counting fields per row against the header (`fix_b34_field_shape.py`: `BEFORE_RAGGED 1 [('B34', 15)]` -> `AFTER_RAGGED 0`, `bytes= 42191 sha256_prefix= 17a89217d7ad509b`); the re-point run then read `sha= 4c39aff8677b48c3`. The per-row column count is now asserted inside the shipped gate (`test_both_csvs_keep_the_packs_own_shape`), and falsified by `falsify_ragged_row_assertion.py`: control exit 0, planted extra column exit 1 naming `('B34', 15)`, file restored with a matching SHA, exit 0 again.
errors.repeat_prevention: Never trust a repair receipt for the bytes another script may still rewrite: after the last write in a chain, re-read the shipped file and re-run the predicate against it, and state the SHA of what the receipt describes. Any tool that edits a CSV, JSON or other delimited artifact as raw text must assert that artifact's own structural invariant after writing -- for a table that means the field count of every row, because a parser that tolerates surplus fields will report a malformed file as a clean one.
errors.remaining_boundary: The new assertion counts fields; it cannot tell whether a field that grew was meant to hold a comma and lose its quoting, or hold a sentence and gain one. The sentence now avoids the delimiter instead of being quoted, which keeps the pack's own unquoted style for that column; a future rewrite that needs commas must add the quotes, and the row-level field count is the tripwire, not the quote style.

errors.observed_error: WUI-18's last unmeasured clause was "the hook returns fast and does not wake a model". Reading the two managed hooks showed why it could not have been claimed: neither `packages/client-neutral-core/bin/hermes-project-terminal-guard.py` nor `packages/client-neutral-core/bin/hermes-project-data.py` passed `timeout=` to a single one of its five `subprocess.run` call sites, and two of those sites are Git metadata lookups (`rev-parse --show-toplevel`, `check-ignore -q --no-index`) that run on every tool call. A locked index, a credential prompt or an enormous work tree therefore sat in front of the whole client with no ceiling, and the failure would have looked like a slow Hermes rather than a stuck `git`. Nothing measured it, because `tests/workflow-assistance/test_project_terminal_guard.py` drives the guard's *policy* with payloads and never its latency.
errors.root_cause: The hooks were written as correctness guards, not as latency-bounded ones: the same `subprocess.run` shape that reads a Git answer was copied into the pre-tool path without anyone asking what happens when that answer never arrives. And the test suite could not have found it -- a shape assertion ("every guard lookup carries a ceiling") had never been written, so the only existing tests passed on a tree where the defect was universal.
errors.fix: The two metadata lookups now carry a declared ceiling (`ROOT_CHECK_TIMEOUT_SECONDS = 5.0` in the guard, `GIT_METADATA_TIMEOUT_SECONDS = 5.0` in the wrapper, both sited against the measured latency) and a timeout is reported as its own reason: the guard raises `RootCheckUnresolved` and refuses with "project root is unresolved (…)", while `is_git_ignored` raises `ProjectDataBoundaryError` naming "ignore status is unproven" -- because returning False on a stall would let a directory through the boundary check that was never proven ignored, and returning None would tell the owner their workdir is not a Git project, which a hung `git` has no authority to claim. The two sites that run the user's own command (`run_command`, `run_kanban_command`) stay unbounded on purpose and are named as such by the test, so the assertion cannot silently widen. Measured with the real toolchain: guard root lookup p50 12.0ms / p95 12.6ms / max 12.6ms against a 5000ms ceiling; the guard *process* end to end (interpreter start included) block path p50 57.9 / p95 69.2 / max 79.1, allow path p50 57.1 / p95 68.8 / max 79.2. "No model wake" is checked structurally: neither hook imports requests, httpx, urllib.request, http.client, socket, openai or anthropic, so no call path exists from a pre-tool hook to a provider. New mandatory gate: `tests/workflow-assistance/test_hooks_answer_within_a_bound_without_waking_a_model.py`, 10 cases green, including a control that forces the real timeout to fire (`project_root(root, timeout=1e-06)` must raise) so the ceiling is known to be reachable, a call-site census floor of 5 so the AST scan cannot pass by seeing nothing, and a positive control that `is_git_ignored` still answers True for `.project-local/runs/probe` and False for `AGENTS.md`. Falsification: removing one `timeout=` from the guard turned the suite red with failures=3 and named `('hermes-project-terminal-guard.py', 'project_root')`; the file was restored by bytes (19,621 B, matching SHA) and 10/10 green again. Regression read in the same tree: `test_project_terminal_guard.py` 29 OK, `test_project_data_boundary.py` 17 OK.
errors.repeat_prevention: Every process a pre-tool hook starts must carry a ceiling, and every "fast" claim must be a number read from the machine; a guard whose lookup can hang is not a guard, it is an outage with a policy message. An unbounded call is allowed only where it is the user's own command, and that exception must be named in the test so it cannot become a catch-all. A timeout must never be reported as a negative answer: "unresolved" and "not a project" are different facts, and collapsing them sends the reader to hunt a defect that does not exist.
errors.remaining_boundary: The ceiling is in the tracked source. The live client runs whatever is deployed in Hermes Home, and ERR-250 measures that this machine has none of the declared overlay `bin/` assets at all, so the bound protects the source today and the installed client only after a sanctioned sync. A ceiling of 5s also means a stuck `git` costs up to 5s per call rather than forever; it is not a retry budget, and no cache of the root answer was added.

errors.observed_error: WUI-18's clause "队列/磁盘有界；轮转截断" had only been met on one side. The collector queue is bounded (`services/orchestration/collector_scheduler.py`, `BoundedEventQueue(max_size=1000)`, drops the oldest heartbeat, never a terminal event), while `canonical_store.py` had no row ceiling, no byte ceiling, no rotation and no pruning of any kind -- the only size-related statement in the file is `PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE)` at close, which reclaims the WAL and leaves the ledger growing forever. Measured by opening a real store and writing 400 telemetry events: 4,057,464 B on disk before any policy existed to bound it. Reading the write path also exposed a defect that the missing feature would have activated: `append_telemetry` derived its `sequence` from `SELECT COUNT(*) + 1`. While nothing ever deleted a row that was harmless, and the column has no reader today -- but the moment retention removed old rows the count dropped, and the next insert would re-issue a sequence value already used. A cursor that repeats is worse than one that gaps: `services/orchestration/sse_revision.py` states SSE ids come from the canonical persistent sequence, and a replayed cursor silently looks like a missed update.
errors.root_cause: Two omissions that travelled together. First, the store was written as a durable ledger with no lifecycle: nothing in it or around it ever asked how big it is or what the ceiling should be, so "bounded" was claimed from the queue and never contradicted by the file. Second, a monotonic counter was implemented as a population count, which is only monotonic while nothing is ever deleted -- the same "derived from a count instead of from the max" mistake that ERR-246 recorded for the triage ceiling, in a different table. The per-insert `COUNT(*)` was also a full-table scan on the hot write path, so the ledger cost grew with its own size.
errors.fix: `CanonicalStore.disk_footprint()` reports `pageSizeBytes`/`pageCount` from SQLite's own pragmas, `logicalDatabaseBytes` (page math) and `databaseFileBytes`/`walBytes`/`shmBytes` from stat, and totals the physical ones -- the two are deliberately separate labels because in WAL mode the logical size counts pages the main file has not absorbed yet, and conflating them makes a reclaim look like it happened when only the WAL moved. `enforce_retention(limits, allow_prune=...)` caps the append-only tables and refuses everything else: `RETAINABLE_TABLES` is **derived** from the shipped `WAL_TABLES` minus `RETENTION_EXEMPT_TABLES = (schema_migrations, projects, tasks)`, so a table added to the ledger later is un-prunable until someone states its category, and `tasks` is exempt because it holds live lease/checkpoint/fencing state rather than history. Ordering uses the `_newest_column` helper already used by the fingerprint witness (shared predicate, so a prune cannot order by a column the witness no longer trusts). `allow_prune=False` returns `wouldDelete` without deleting, so the cost of a ceiling is visible before it is granted. `append_telemetry` now derives `sequence` from `COALESCE(MAX(sequence),0)+1`. `services/orchestration/durable_worker.py` exposes the grant as `--retention-rows table=N[,table=N]`, validating it at the CLI as well as in the store, applying it at startup and after a `--once` tick, and printing both sweeps inside the run payload. Measured: 390 of 400 rows pruned under a 10-row ceiling, `bytes_before=4,057,464 bytes_after=397,312 reclaimed=3,660,152` (90.2%), with the survivor set verified as the newest rows by the very column the report names. New mandatory gate: `tests/workflow-assistance/test_canonical_store_disk_is_bounded.py`, 10 cases green -- refusals delete nothing, dry-run deletes nothing, a second table is bounded by the same call so the feature is not telemetry-only, and the sequence control asserts the value still rises across a prune. Falsification: dropping `tasks` from the exemption list turned the suite red (`FAIL: test_a_ceiling_for_a_table_that_may_not_be_pruned_is_refused_without_deleting`, RAN=10 FAILURES=1) and the file was restored byte-identically (58,952 B, matching SHA) before re-greening. Regression read in the same tree with the gate's own module pythonpath: `test_canonical_store`, `test_durable_worker`, `test_canonical_store_v2`, `test_changed_scope_canonical_wiring`, `test_worker_runtime_roots_stay_inside_the_project` -- 34 + 18 cases, 0 failures.
errors.repeat_prevention: A durable store must state its own ceiling and report its size in the unit the operator cares about, because an unbounded ledger turns a "low overhead" claim into a disk incident owned by someone else. Any counter derived from a population count must be re-examined before anything is ever deleted, and monotonic values must come from MAX, not COUNT. Pruning eligibility must be derived from a shipped table list plus a stated exemption, never from a hand-copied set, so a new table defaults to un-prunable. Report logical and physical size separately: a checkpoint that only moves the WAL must not read as reclaimed bytes.
errors.remaining_boundary: The daemon loop has no post-tick hook, so a long-running `run_forever()` worker prunes only at startup; the ceiling is enforced per process launch, and closing that gap needs a hook on the worker loop rather than a longer flag list. Nothing here sets a default ceiling: `--retention-rows` unset means the store still grows, because choosing the number is an owner/product decision about how much history the Observer is allowed to lose, and a default invented in code would silently delete evidence. The reclaimed-byte figure is one run on one store under one ceiling, not a projected steady-state growth rate.

errors.observed_error: The citation gate I hardened this session turned red on a file that exists. Four matrix rows cite `packages/client-neutral-core/scripts/operation_progress.py`, the producer written minutes earlier, and the gate reported `resolves to no file` for each. `file_index()` built its population from `git ls-files` plus a **hand-listed** set of directories (`scripts/audit`, `apps/observer/frontend/src`, `docs/current/ui-priority-20261009`, `packages/contracts/schemas/workflow`, `tests/workflow-assistance`) -- the module root where workflow code actually lives was never in that list, so every untracked file under `packages/client-neutral-core/scripts/` and `services/` was invisible to a guard whose whole job is to say whether a path exists. The same list had already acquitted or convicted by accident: it worked earlier only because the paths cited so far happened to fall inside those five directories.
errors.root_cause: An existence check was given a partial universe. The index was widened once already this session (the document-citation guard had the identical defect and was fixed by walking the tree), but the fix did not travel to the second gate, and neither gate asserted that its population is larger than the tracked file list -- so a directory list that stops covering new roots shrinks silently and every red it prints looks like a data error rather than a scope error.
errors.fix: `file_index()` now takes `git ls-files` union a repo-wide `os.walk`, pruning during traversal: `.project-local`, `.ui-reference`, `node_modules`, `dist`, `.git`, `__pycache__`, `.venv`, `target`, `build`. Pruning happens in `dirnames` rather than after the fact because walking into `.project-local` would read another machine's toolchain before answering, and the first version of that predicate required a non-empty relative path, so `.project-local` at the top of the tree was never pruned -- the new case caught it on the same turn. The runtime root is still checked separately by `test_a_runtime_receipt_citation_is_not_invented`, because a runtime file is verifiable on the machine that wrote it and not in a fresh checkout. Added `test_the_index_is_the_checkout_and_not_a_list_of_directories_i_thought_of`: the index must be strictly larger than the tracked list, must contain the producer this session added, and the walked half must contain no `.project-local/` path. Windows detail worth keeping: reading `git ls-files` with `text=True` and no `encoding=` hands the pipe to cp936, the reader thread dies on a Chinese path, and the call still returns code 0 with `stdout=None` -- the comparison would have run against an empty tracked set and passed for the wrong reason, so the call decodes bytes explicitly now. Measured after the fix: 8 cases green, 234 citations resolving, 144 line pointers compared against file bodies with 0 problems. Falsification: re-pruning the walk to the old directory list brought back 7 unresolved citations and turned the population case red (`FAILED (failures=2)`), and the file was restored byte-identically (20,973 B, matching SHA) before re-greening (`.project-local/runs/wui-20261010/falsify_widened_file_index.py`).
errors.repeat_prevention: A check that answers "does this exist" must state the universe it searched and assert that universe is bigger than the narrowest thing it replaced; a population built from a list of directories I thought of is a scope bug waiting for the next new root. When one gate is fixed for a partial-population defect, find the other gates with the same shape in the same session -- the defect travelled twice here. On Windows, never read subprocess output with text=True and no encoding=.
errors.remaining_boundary: Widening the index makes it more permissive about *existence*: a path that exists only as a vendored copy inside the checkout would now resolve. Frozen and reference trees are pruned for that reason, but the gate still answers "is there a file here", not "is this the file the sentence means" -- the line-pointer content check is what carries that, and it abstains on citations that quote no code.

errors.observed_error: The governance batch turned red on a module that had been green for every previous run: `test_the_context_pack_moves_only_its_generation_stamp_between_renders` rendered the handoff pack twice in one batch and got two different `Content SHA-256` values (`afb6bdb88af040af` vs `eccc8ca23e3907a2`), with every other line identical. The pack's own header promises the digest is its content identity so a session can quote the material it loaded; in fact the digest was computed over the whole rendered body **including the `- Generated UTC:` line**, so it changed on every render. The gate that was supposed to catch that compared two renders and excluded the stamp line -- which means it only ever passed while both renders landed inside the same second.
errors.root_cause: A content hash was taken over a document that contains a timestamp. The test then papered over it by excluding exactly that timestamp line from the comparison, so the arrangement was self-consistent as long as the process was fast: two renders in the same second give the same stamp, hence the same digest, hence a green run. Nothing in the system asserted the property that matters -- same content, same digest -- across time. This session made the pack slower to render (a larger register and the new contracts read into it), the two renders straddled a second boundary, and a latent defect in the provenance surfaced as a batch failure caused by an unrelated-looking change.
errors.fix: `build_context_pack.py` now hashes a body with the `- Generated UTC:` line removed, beside the `filled-after-render` placeholder it already excluded, and states why in a comment at the call site so nobody re-adds the stamp to the digest for tidiness. The stamp keeps being printed, so provenance about *when* is intact while provenance about *what* becomes stable. Measured with six renders a second apart: `renders=6 distinct_digests=1 distinct_stamps=6 body_chars=[11954]` (`.project-local/runs/wui-20261010/prove_pack_digest_stable_across_seconds_v2.py`). The pre-fix claim is measured rather than assumed: recomputing the old formula over four rendered bodies gives four different digests (`25cf1006facaebef`, `a7a1bc62d244e6a5`, `ba9cea4fdfc3aaec`, `eaeea6ca4ce6574d`) while the shipped formula gives one (`d7ef1321edeba540`) (`.project-local/runs/wui-20261010/falsify_pack_digest_fix.py`). The affected module then read `OK` and the batch is being re-run to confirm. Windows detail caught while writing the proof: the pack subprocess emits CRLF, so a `$`-anchored regex silently matched nothing while the render still returned exit 0 -- the probe had to normalise the newlines before it could claim anything.
errors.repeat_prevention: A content digest must never cover a wall-clock value; if a document carries both, hash the body and print the stamp. And a stability test that compares two renders in the same second is not a stability test -- assert the invariant across a time boundary, or state in the test that it only proves within-second equality. Anything that makes a rendering slower can expose a latent timing assumption, so a new red in an untouched module is a lead to chase, not noise to re-run away.
errors.remaining_boundary: The six-render proof runs in one process against one working tree; it does not make the digest stable across commits (the body legitimately changes when the register or a source file changes, which is the point). Nothing here binds the digest to a git object: HEAD is printed separately and is the commit-side fact.

errors.observed_error: The TypeScript projection that the frontend and Rust are told to consume instead of hand-forking contract shapes rendered every JSON-Schema `enum` as a fixed-length TUPLE, and dropped every `const`. Counted over the bytes at HEAD (`packages/client-neutral-core/generated/contracts.ts`, 32,527 B / 1,004 lines): 77 tuple-typed enum fields, 0 union-typed fields, 40 `Record<string, unknown>` collapses. Two shipped lines say it better than a description: `status: ["PENDING", "APPROVED", "REJECTED"]` (HEAD:67) — a value that is one of three literals is not a three-element array — and `operation_modes: ["MANAGE", "OBSERVE", "IGNORE", "FORBIDDEN"][]` (HEAD:155), where the `[]` was applied to the tuple because array-of-enum precedence was never handled. `MAX_DEPTH = 2` collapsed anything three levels down, so the snapshot's own `projects` field read `projects: Record<string, unknown>[]` (HEAD:227) — the projection named nothing about the row it is supposed to type. Reproduced by putting HEAD's bytes back and running the content gate against them: exit=1, first refusals `action-plan lost the const 'workflow/action-plan/v1' on schema_version` and `Lists differ: [] != [('action-plan', '"DRAFT" | "WAITING_APPRO...')]` (`.project-local/runs/wui-20261010/prove_generator_projection_and_idempotence.py`). No gate was red while any of this shipped, because `verify_contract_ssot.py` proves the SET of @contract markers equals the catalog and never looks at a body.
errors.root_cause: The generator was written for 'practical depth' and its output was verified by counting markers. A marker count is satisfied by a file that types nothing, so the only existing check could not distinguish 'the projection is complete' from 'the projection exists'. The enum case was implemented as the JSON array literal rather than as the type the values inhabit, and `const` had no branch at all, so it fell through to the collapse.
errors.fix: `_ts_type` now projects `enum` as a union of literals (`"A" | "B"`), `const` as the literal itself, parenthesises an array of a union (`("A"|"B")[]`), and dedupes the type-plus-enum-null combination; `MAX_DEPTH` went 2 -> 5. Regenerated in place: 43,269 B / 1,293 lines / 99 union-typed lines / 28 collapses, and sha bfba4de2a5f8e087 -- re-running the generator reproduces that sha byte-identically, so the shipped file is generator output and not a hand-tuned projection that happens to satisfy its own gate. The 3 remaining tuple-shaped lines were traced rather than assumed: each is a genuine `const` array (`packages/contracts/schemas/workflow/adapter-registry.schema.json:18`, `client-adapter.schema.json:18`), where a fixed tuple IS the correct type. New guard `tests/workflow-assistance/test_generated_contract_types_project_the_schema.py` (9 cases) compiles the generated file with `tsc --noEmit --strict` and refuses a planted TS2322, and compares TransportState / FamilyState / GitMatchState / CostQuality member-for-member against the hand-written `apps/observer/frontend/src/types.ts`.
errors.repeat_prevention: A generator's output must be asserted on CONTENT, never on markers alone: prove the generated file compiles with the type checker its consumer uses, prove each enum arrives as a union, and prove regeneration is idempotent against the shipped bytes. Any projection that collapses a name into `Record<string, unknown>` must be counted and the count must be allowed to go DOWN, not merely be tolerated. When a remaining collapse is reported, trace it to the schema construct that causes it before calling it correct.
errors.remaining_boundary: Nesting deeper than five levels still collapses (28 lines measured); that is the generator's documented limit, not a proof of harmlessness. No Rust readback was produced for this file in this round -- the docstring says frontend/Rust consume it, and only the frontend side (tsc strict) was exercised. Exact-SHA CI evidence is owed because nothing here has been committed or pushed.

errors.observed_error: WUI-18's poison-row clause was recorded as "an undecided design question", and the code shows why both existing behaviours were wrong in opposite directions. `DurableWorker.run_once` wrote rows in a bare loop (`for record in outcome.records: self._write_record(...)`) with no per-row guard, so ONE row that the store refuses -- a foreign `usage.jsonl` line whose `provider` carries a credential shape, refused by `validate_record` since ERR-244 -- raised out of the loop, hit the collector-level `except Exception`, marked the collector `ok=False`, and DROPPED EVERY ROW AFTER IT in that collector. The canary gate had already to prove the opposite property for the planted secret (`an honest line must not be collateral damage`, `test_canary_synthetic_secret_never_reaches_the_store.py:113`), and did it with its own per-row try/except, so the production path stayed unguarded. errors.fix: Per-row isolation with first-class refusal accounting. `DurableWorker._write_records` writes row by row and returns `(stored, refusals_by_reason, first_sample_per_reason)`; the reason key is the exception class plus its leading clause so a sensitive-name refusal and a shape refusal are not the same number, and the sample is the FIRST place it happened, not the newest symptom. Health semantics stay honest: a collector whose every row was refused is `ok=False` and increments `consecutive_failures`, because nothing got through; three of four rows landing is a delivered source with a counted debt. Refusals ACCUMULATE into `collector_health.refused_rows` (migration version 4, with `last_refusal_reason`) so a clean tick cannot launder the debt, and the tick payload reports `stored`/`refused`/`refusalReasons`/`refusalSamples`. On the client, the cursor was mirrored locally and mirrored values drift from their authority -- here the platform's own `EventSource.lastEventId` -- and the reset-on-error made the local copy wrong exactly when it was supposed to matter. Because no test ever dropped a live connection, neither half was ever exercised end to end.
errors.fix: SERVER: the empty-ring branch moved AFTER the future-cursor check and now answers a real gap with `resync_required` / `history_unavailable_after_restart` carrying the watermark, while a cursor already AT the watermark is honestly silent (nothing was missed, so nothing may be claimed). CLIENT: the local mirror is gone -- `openEventStream` reads the platform's cursor through a named local type (`EventSourceWithCursor`, because this project's `lib` surface does not declare the standard property), `onOpen` fires only for the first open and `onReconnect(cursor)` for every later one, and the error handler reports the interruption without touching the socket: closing the source on error would forfeit the browser's automatic reconnect and the cursor with it. The call site now supplies both handlers and keeps the conservative re-read per open -- one read per open, never two, since the two paths are mutually exclusive by construction.
